damage_scenario: The EKS Kubernetes API server is the single control-plane entry point through which every deployment, scaling operation, pod restart, configuration change, and secret rotation in the ap-south-1 cluster is requested, while the running pods themselves keep serving traffic without it. If its availability is compromised, no workload in the cluster can be created, changed, restarted, or rolled back for the duration of the outage, so a failed, defective, or security-relevant release of the connected-vehicle diagnostic and telemetry backend remains in place exactly as it is and cannot be corrected until the control plane answers again.

The EKS Kubernetes API server is the enforcement point that evaluates Kubernetes RBAC bindings together with IAM/OIDC identity on every request to decide which namespaces, resources, and actions a user, group, or service account is permitted to take. If its authorization is compromised, an identity that is properly authenticated but holds only narrow rights — a contractor account, a CI pipeline credential, or a single-namespace developer role — can create, modify, and delete workloads and read secrets in production namespaces it was never entitled to touch, so the team, environment, and production-versus-test boundaries that RBAC exists to enforce are no longer respected and no permission review record can be trusted.

The EKS worker nodes are the compute substrate on which every platform pod runs, so they hold diagnostic and vehicle data in transit along with material that exists nowhere else — API keys, TLS private keys and refresh tokens loaded into pod memory — and each node additionally serves its kubelet and instance metadata endpoint. If the confidentiality of these worker nodes is compromised, that material can be read directly from node memory or through the exposed instance metadata endpoint, so the data exchanged for a single diagnostic session — including vehicle VIN, fault and telemetry content belonging to one identifiable vehicle owner — is disclosed even though it was never intended to leave the cluster.

The EKS worker nodes are the runtime that executes all platform workloads, so the container images, binaries and pod configurations resident on them define what the platform actually computes from vehicle data and what it does with update packages. If the integrity of these worker nodes is compromised, the code and configuration the platform executes can be substituted or altered on the node, and the platform then returns altered diagnostic results, processes altered OTA content, or stores altered vehicle data in the databases, with no reliable means of telling its own approved logic apart from logic that was changed underneath it.

The Envoy Gateway and its NLB are the only path by which external API traffic enters the cloud platform, terminating TLS, validating client identity, and routing each request to the specific backend service that issued the credential. If its integrity is compromised, no one can trust that the requests reaching the backends are the ones the original caller actually sent under the identity they claim — a diagnostic command payload or a service-to-service call can be altered in transit, or delivered to a different backend than the one that authorized it, while the platform's own logs still record the original content and the original caller.

All internet traffic to the cloud API funnels through this single NLB and Envoy pair, which terminate TLS and forward every request to the in-cluster services, so no consumer has an alternate route in or out of the platform. If its availability is compromised, the entire public API becomes unreachable at once — remote diagnostics, vehicle provisioning, license checks, and update orchestration all stop working simultaneously for every external caller, and no backend service can be reached through any other path.

The Kong API gateway is the single front door for the cloud API, running the authentication plugins, rate limiting and routing for /core/v2, /data/v2 and /pandora/v1, and it is the point that binds every request to the specific dealership, vehicle and user scope the caller is entitled to. If its authorization is compromised, an identity that passed authentication legitimately is granted scopes it was never issued, so a technician or tenant account is served another dealership's vehicle records, diagnostic results and license identifiers through the normal gateway path, because nothing at the gateway stops the call from crossing a tenant or vehicle ownership boundary.

The Hasura GraphQL engine is the front door to the core database, and its role and tenant permission rules are the mechanism that confines each caller's queries to the specific rows, columns, and records their access level permits. If its authorization is compromised, those row- and field-level rules no longer hold, and requests made under one tenant's role return or modify records belonging to a different tenant, so data kept in separate customer groups or dealer networks is no longer reliably separated.

The Aurora cloudapi database is the system of record for role assignments, authorization policies and tenant-to-dealership bindings, and the Cloud API front door reads these records on every request to decide what a caller may see and do. If the integrity of this data store is compromised, the stored records can no longer be trusted to state what was actually approved, so an access rule that was never authorized — a technician elevated to fleet-wide access, or a dealership's records re-bound to another tenant — can sit in the database and be enforced as if it were legitimate, and the platform has no way to distinguish a correctly configured permission from a falsified one.

This database is the single record the update-instruction signing service consults to determine which ECU software version is currently installed on each vehicle and which vehicle list each OTA campaign is authorized to target. If the integrity of that state is compromised, the signing service can act on a falsified version entry or an altered campaign target list and still produce correctly signed update instructions, so vehicles outside the campaign or running an ineligible software baseline are treated as valid recipients, and the stored version history stops reflecting what is actually installed on each vehicle.

The Aurora PostgreSQL database is the system of record for which vehicle identities are enrolled in the fleet and which device certificate each identity is bound to, and every provisioning, authentication, and entitlement decision is read from these rows. If its integrity is compromised, the stored enrollment and certificate-binding records silently diverge from the real enrollment state, so the platform treats a revoked, never-enrolled, or misassigned device certificate as valid and processes provisioning requests against the wrong vehicle identity, resulting in legitimate vehicles being refused updates and diagnostics while unauthorized devices are provisioned as correctly enrolled hardware.
